entity: older adults, young children, people with chronic illness and households without air conditioning
business_impact: Federal weather guidance says young children and infants, older adults, people with chronic medical conditions and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to heat, and advises checking in on friends and relatives in these groups, especially if they do not have air conditioning.
story_seed: A heat index of 103°F or higher is forecast for {metro} on two or more days in a row — a Weather Company meteorologist on how hot, how long and whether nights cool off, for families checking on older relatives, young children and neighbors without air conditioning

evidence.source: National Weather Service, "Heat Safety Tips and Resources"

entity: pedestrians, older adults and emergency departments
business_impact: A study by a city health department in Philadelphia found that snow was the weather condition most associated with days of unusually high emergency department visits for falls, with the snow typically a couple of days before, and that many of those falls happened in the morning, apparently on the way to work.
story_seed: An inch or more of snow is forecast for {metro} — a Weather Company meteorologist on when it falls and how much, for people walking to work and school over the next few mornings

evidence.source: Gevitz et al., "Risk of Fall-Related Injury due to Adverse Weather Events, Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, 2006-2011," Public Health Reports 132(1 Suppl), 2017

entity: older adults, people with chronic illness and households without air conditioning in places where heat is unusual
business_impact: A study of hospital admissions in 22 states found that heat-related admissions begin to rise at moderately hot heat index values, defined for each county by its own summer climate, which in some cooler regions were below the levels then used for heat alerts, and its authors flag people in cooler places without air conditioning as a particular concern.
story_seed: A spell of heat well above normal for {metro}, with a heat index of 95°F or more on two or more days, is in the forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on how hot, how long and whether nights cool off, for people checking on older relatives and neighbors without air conditioning

evidence.source: Vaidyanathan et al., "Assessment of extreme heat and hospitalizations to inform early warning systems," Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 116(12), 2019

entity: people at risk of mosquito-borne illness and local health departments
business_impact: A study of more than 16,000 West Nile virus cases reported to federal health authorities in 17 states found that a week with at least one day of 50 mm (about 2 inches) or more of rain was followed by a higher incidence of reported West Nile infection that week and over the next two weeks.
story_seed: A day with 2 inches or more of rain is forecast for {metro} during mosquito season — a Weather Company meteorologist on how much falls and where water may stand afterward, for health departments and families thinking about mosquito bites in the weeks ahead

evidence.source: Soverow et al., "Infectious Disease in a Warming World: How Weather Influenced West Nile Virus in the United States (2001–2005)," Environmental Health Perspectives 117(7), 2009

entity: people who rely on electricity-dependent medical equipment at home
business_impact: Federal health preparedness guidance says power outages caused by a major emergency can last longer and be life-threatening for people who depend on home-use medical devices, and advises identifying backup power sources for medical equipment and keeping chargers and power banks for home-use devices ready.
story_seed: Severe thunderstorms are likely in the {metro} forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on when the strongest storms arrive and how long they last, for people who use home oxygen, home dialysis or other powered medical equipment and are checking their backup power

evidence.source: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Prepare Your Health, "Power Sources" (2024)

entity: people with asthma and emergency departments
business_impact: A study in Louisiana found that on thunderstorm days emergency department visits for asthma rose with heavier rain, mainly among children and adults under 65, and its authors suggest people with asthma consider precautions during thunderstorms and emergency departments consider preparing for forecast thunderstorm days.
story_seed: Thunderstorms with an inch or more of precipitation are forecast for {metro} — a Weather Company meteorologist on when the storms arrive and how long they last, for people with asthma and local emergency departments

evidence.source: Park et al., "Associations of Emergency Department Visits for Asthma with Precipitation and Temperature on Thunderstorm Days: A Time-Series Analysis of Data from Louisiana, USA, 2010–2012," Environmental Health Perspectives 130(8), 2022

entity: households using generators and fuel-burning heaters after ice storms
business_impact: A federal and state investigation of a 2009 Kentucky ice storm found that carbon monoxide poisonings from generators and kerosene and propane heaters followed the storm's power outages, peaking two to four days afterward while temperatures stayed below freezing, with the highest rates where the most ice had accumulated.
story_seed: A quarter inch or more of freezing rain is forecast for {metro} — a Weather Company meteorologist on how much ice, when it ends and how cold the days after will be, for households that may turn to generators or fuel-burning heaters

evidence.source: Lutterloh et al., "Carbon Monoxide Poisoning After an Ice Storm in Kentucky, 2009," Public Health Reports 126(Suppl 1), 2011

entity: people shoveling snow, especially those with heart disease or heart risk factors
business_impact: A national heart-health organization says the exertion of shoveling heavy snow may raise the risk of a heart attack or sudden cardiac arrest, citing a study in Canada in which about 7 to 8 inches of snow was linked to higher odds of men being hospitalized with or dying from a heart attack, and says people with heart disease or heart risk factors should take particular care.
story_seed: Eight inches or more of snow is forecast for {metro} — a Weather Company meteorologist on how much, how heavy and wet, and when it ends, for people planning to clear driveways and sidewalks

evidence.source: American Heart Association, "Snow shoveling can be hazardous to your heart" (news release, Dec. 15, 2022)

entity: pedestrians and older adults on icy sidewalks
business_impact: Freezing rain can glaze sidewalks, steps and driveways, making slips and falls more likely for anyone who has to walk outside.
story_seed: Freezing rain is in the {metro} forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on when it starts and stops and how long temperatures stay below freezing afterward, for people who need to walk outside

entity: older adults and mobile-home residents in severe-storm country
business_impact: The highest severe-thunderstorm risk level is in the forecast, and storms at that level can produce tornadoes; older adults and people in mobile homes may need more time and help to reach a safe room, so knowing where to shelter ahead of time matters.
story_seed: The highest severe-storm risk level is forecast for {metro} — a Weather Company meteorologist on when the strongest storms arrive, especially if they come after dark, for families helping older relatives and neighbors in mobile homes plan where to shelter

entity: people experiencing homelessness, outreach teams and households without heat
business_impact: A study by the New York City health department found that most cold-related deaths happened outdoors, many among people experiencing homelessness, and that about a third occurred on or just after the coldest nights of the season for the city, while indoor cold deaths occurred in homes without heat.
story_seed: One of the coldest nights of the season for {metro} is in the forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on how cold, how long and when it eases, for shelters, outreach teams and people checking on neighbors without heat

evidence.source: Lane et al. 2018, New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene, "Burden and Risk Factors for Cold-Related Illness and Death in New York City"

entity: older adults, especially in high-poverty neighborhoods and homes without air conditioning
business_impact: A study of more than 73 million older Medicare beneficiaries found that runs of nights much warmer than usual for the area were linked to more deaths that year from heart, lung and brain conditions, especially in high-poverty neighborhoods.
story_seed: Two or more nights far warmer than normal for {metro} are in the forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on how warm the nights stay and when relief arrives, for people checking on older relatives without air conditioning

evidence.source: Healy et al. 2026, "Heat waves and annual mortality among older adults (aged ≥65 years) in the USA", Lancet Planetary Health

entity: people prone to kidney stones and the clinicians who treat them
business_impact: A study of kidney stone visits in five US cities found that hot days, with average temperatures around 86°F, were followed within a few days by more people seeking care for kidney stones than on mild days.
story_seed: A run of very warm days and nights, unusually hot even for {metro}, is in the forecast — a Weather Company meteorologist on how hot and for how long, for people prone to kidney stones and the clinicians who treat them

evidence.source: Tasian et al. 2014, "Daily Mean Temperature and Clinical Kidney Stone Presentation in Five U.S. Metropolitan Areas", Environmental Health Perspectives
